title: The Arena
description: Three challenges, real Python, real simulation. This is everything Module 10 taught you, aimed at something harder than any single lesson asked for.

content.value: Each challenge below drops you into a world you've seen before, but without a lesson walking you through the exact solution. Fewer ticks used to reach the goal is a rough stand-in for a leaderboard's "time" — a tighter, more direct program beats a meandering one.
Navigate the obstacle field to the goal, as directly as you can.

content.title: 🏁 Maze Sprint

content.value: Follow the track to the goal at the far end. Both sensors need to work together — check back on Module 7's line-following rules if it's been a while.

content.title: 🏁 Line Race

content.value: A tighter, more maze-like obstacle course. The starting heading is different from the other two challenges — read it carefully before you write your first move.

content.title: 🏁 Warehouse Run

content.value: None of the three starter programs shown are optimal — they're deliberately plain starting points, the same way this course has never handed you a finished answer. Tightening the turn angles and thresholds is the actual challenge.
Key takeaway: the arena is every idea from Modules 5 through 10, applied without a lesson holding your hand — real sensing, real decisions, real code, on three different layouts.

quiz.question: What does 'fewer ticks used' approximate in the arena challenges?
options: A rough stand-in for time — a tighter, more direct program reaches the goal faster
The number of lines of code written
quiz.explain: Since each tick is a fixed simulated time step, fewer ticks to the goal means a more efficient run — the same idea a real leaderboard would measure by wall-clock time.

quiz.question: Why does the Line Race challenge require checking both robot.line() sensors together, rather than just one?
options: It doesn't — one sensor is enough
Two sensors reading together tell you whether the robot is centred, drifted left, drifted right, or has lost the line entirely — Module 7's four-case rule table
robot.line() only works with two sensors checked separately
quiz.explain: This is exactly the same two-sensor logic Module 7 built by hand — now expressed as real Python conditions.
